extracted.intended_audience: hospital coders, device manufacturers, health policy analysts, and other stakeholders involved in Medicare IPPS/LTCH MS-DRG classification and rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating, reassigning, and subdividing ICD-10-PCS procedure codes into MS-DRGs (including creation/deletion of MS-DRGs and severity-level splits) using claims data, clinical coherence, and resource-utilization criteria for the IPPS/LTCH PPS rulemaking process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical coherence for grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures and devices grouped to an MS-DRG should be clinically coherent (share similar clinical characteristics and intended clinical function).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a procedure/device is clinically similar to existing members of an MS-DRG (example: WiSE® CRT System electrode aligns with leadless pacemakers because both eliminate traditional wire-based leads). Clinical coherence is a primary rationale for reassigning procedure codes between MS-DRGs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource-utilization alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: MS-DRG membership and potential reassignments should reflect alignment in resource consumption (costs, length of stay, other hospital resources) across grouped cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use claims data (e.g., MedPAR) to compare average costs and length of stay; if resource utilization is comparable across categories, consider restructuring MS-DRGs (for example, deleting older subdivisions if replacement and revision procedures now use similar resources).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of MedPAR claims data for evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions about MS-DRG assignments and subgrouping are based on analysis of MedPAR claims data updates (e.g., September updates) to assess volumes, costs, and lengths of stay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine current and multi-year MedPAR files to identify case counts, average LOS, average costs, and trends. Present findings in tables and simulations supporting proposed reassignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer substantial case volume for MS-DRG stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer MS-DRGs to have a substantial number of cases because larger, clinically cohesive groups provide greater stability for annual updates to relative payment weights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If very few patients are in an MS-DRG, analyze clinical characteristics, treatment patterns, and resource utilization to determine whether to propose modifications or reclassifications; low volume alone may trigger further analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-year data comparison to avoid single-year fluctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use at least two years of MedPAR claims data when determining whether additional severity levels or splits are warranted to avoid decisions driven by isolated yearly fluctuations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare data from two consecutive FY MedPAR file updates (e.g., September 2024 and September 2025) when validating established severity levels and supporting changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five statutory/analytic criteria to create severity subgroups
rubrics_metrics.description: All five specified criteria must be met for a base MS-DRG to be split into severity-level subgroups (used for deciding three-way or two-way splits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The five criteria (as applied for two-way 'with MCC' vs 'without MCC' splits) are: (1) at least 500 cases in each subgroup; (2) each subgroup constitutes at least 5% of base MS-DRG cases; (3) at least a 20% difference in average costs between subgroups; (4) at least a $2,000 difference in average costs between subgroups; and (5) at least a 3% reduction in cost variance (improvement in explanatory power) when the split is applied. Apply these criteria in order; if three-way fails, evaluate two-way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-way split specific thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria for a three-way severity split include minimal subgroup size and cost-difference thresholds analogous to the five criteria framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a three-way split (MCC, CC, NonCC) specifically, there must be at least 5% of cases in each subgroup and generally at least 500 cases per subgroup; additionally the relevant cost-difference thresholds (for example, a 20% difference between CC and NonCC) must be met. If any criterion fails, a three-way split should not be adopted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outlier identification in cost/LOS analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and consider unusually expensive or long-stay cases as outliers when interpreting average cost and LOS comparisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outliers may be cases with costs greatly exceeding MS-DRG averages (example: >$100,000) and LOS twice or more than the MS-DRG average. Such cases can skew averages and should be noted or treated as outliers in analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure code reporting logic and clustering effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The GROUPER logic, surgical hierarchy, and whether a procedure code is reported standalone or as part of a cluster affect MS-DRG assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some procedure codes only map to a spinal-fusion MS-DRG when reported with another fusion code on the same claim; reassignment analyses must account for standalone vs cluster reporting, GROUPER logic, and surgical hierarchy (see Section II.C.14 discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of predecessor code assignments and related factors
rubrics_metrics.description: When assigning new or revised procedure codes, review predecessor codes' MS-DRG assignment and designation while considering severity, treatment difficulty, complexity of service, and resources used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This established process includes initial review of predecessor code assignments and public availability of finalized assignments; stakeholders can provide feedback for the following fiscal year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple measures for comparison (avg LOS, avg cost, case counts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare average length of stay, average costs, and case counts by severity level when assessing group comparability or the need for MS-DRG modification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present comparisons by severity (MCC, CC, NonCC) and examine whether differences are comparable to similar MS-DRGs (examples given where average LOS and costs were compared between MS-DRG pairs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Process for proposing reassignments or creating/deleting MS-DRGs
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals to reassign procedure codes, delete existing MS-DRGs, or create new MS-DRGs should be supported by data analysis showing clinical coherence and resource alignment and must follow established rulemaking and public comment processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example actions: reassign ICD-10-PCS codes (e.g., X2HN37B) between MS-DRGs to improve clinical coherence and resource accounting; delete obsolete MS-DRGs and create new MS-DRGs with severity splits when supported by the five criteria and data. Refer to supporting tables (e.g., Table 6P.2a) and CMS website links for code lists and GROUPER logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of clinical indications and principal diagnosis MDC assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect procedure codes tied to specific diagnoses to group to the MDC that contains those diagnoses; MS-DRG assignment is influenced by principal diagnosis MDC (e.g., MDC 01 vs MDC 08).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing procedure code frequency and appropriateness for MS-DRGs, account for the diagnostic MDC that drives grouping; low counts in some MDCs may be expected if indications map primarily to a different MDC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public comment timing and incorporation
rubrics_metrics.description: Public comments on Spring procedure code updates and rule proposals are solicited and considered before final code decisions are made and published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deadlines (example: April 17, 2026 for Spring 2026 procedure code update comments) determine when final code decisions become available to be included in rule tables; finalized codes may be footnoted in published tables and are subject to subsequent public feedback for the following fiscal year.
